Redox mediators and microaeration boosting the linear alkylbenzene 
sulfonate removal
Maurício Guimar˜aes de Oliveira
, Vicente Elício Porfiro Sales Gonçalves da Silva ,  
Steven Renato Ferreira Vasconcelos
, Andr´e Bezerra dos Santos *
Department of Hydraulic and Environmental Engineering, Federal University of Cear´a, Fortaleza, Cear´a, Brazil
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• AQS and microaeration acted synergis­
tically, enabling LAS removal above 
90% in UASB.
• Microaeration increased the specific 
methane yield per COD applied.
• AQS enriched Methanobacterium, sup­
porting a quinone-mediated redox cycle 
mode.
• The combined strategy reshaped the 
microbial community, enriching syntro­
phic bacteria.
• Microaeration increased microbial rich­
ness and diversity.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
UASB reactor
Redox mediator
Syntrophic interactions
Recalcitrant compounds
Biotransformation
A B S T R A C T
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) is one of the most widely used anionic surfactants and is frequently detected 
in wastewater, while its removal under anaerobic conditions remains limited and unstable. This study evaluated 
the independent and combined effects of the redox mediator anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) and controlled 
microaeration on LAS biodegradation in upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactors. Two reactors treating 
synthetic wastewater containing 15 mg L−1 LAS were operated for 90 days: R1, a strictly anaerobic UASB, and 
R2, a micro-aerated UASB. Each reactor was assessed without (Period I) and with AQS addition (50 μM, Period 
II). Under strictly anaerobic conditions without AQS, LAS removal was low and highly unstable (32 ± 16%), with 
pronounced performance fluctuations. The addition of AQS alone significantly improved LAS removal to 65 ±
4% without affecting methane production, indicating enhanced LAS transformation via electron shuttling rather 
than changes in methanogenic activity. Microaeration combined with AQS yielded the best overall performance, 
increasing LAS removal to 77 ± 1%, COD removal to 92.3 ± 3.8%, total methane production to 5.6 ± 0.7 L/day, 
and specific methane yield to 0.50 ± 0.11 LCH4⋅gCODapp
−1 . Microaeration without AQS improved process stability 
but did not achieve LAS removal comparable to AQS. Microbial analyses showed that AQS promoted the 
enrichment of hydrogenotrophic methanogens, particularly Methanobacterium, and syntrophic taxa such as 
midas_g_2229, while microaeration increased microbial richness. The combined condition exhibited the highest 
archaeal enrichment and microbial richness. Results demonstrate that AQS and microaeration act through

1. Introduction
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) is the most widely used anionic 
surfactant (Palmer and Hatley, 2018; Wang et al., 2024). It is a primary 
ingredient in many household and industrial products, including 
laundry detergents, cleaning agents, and personal care products (Ran 
et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2020). Because LAS is widely used and not 
completely removed by conventional wastewater treatment plants 
(WWTPs), it is often found in final effluents and in nearby water bodies. 
Even low concentrations in aquatic environments raise concerns about 
persistence, toxicity, and bioaccumulation. Research shows toxicity at 
levels of at least 15 μg/L (Luo et al., 2023).
LAS is biodegradable under certain conditions, but its degradation in 
WWTPs is often incomplete, especially under anaerobic conditions 
(Ogawa and Kawase, 2021). Commercial LAS mixtures are complex, 
containing homologues of varying alkyl chain lengths and positional 
isomers, which make the compounds resistant to biological treatment, 
particularly in the absence of oxygen (Terreros-Mecalco et al., 2024). At 
moderate to high concentrations, LAS can inhibit microbial activity and 
affect treatment performance (Wu et al., 2020). Concentrations around 
2 mg/L are already sufficient to inhibit nitrifying bacteria (Dereszewska 
et al., 2015), while denitrifying microorganisms are inhibited at 15 
mg/L (Andrade et al., 2020).
In anaerobic systems, which are increasingly used for wastewater 
treatment due to their energy-efficient operation and biogas production, 
LAS removal is typically lower and more variable than in aerobic pro­
cesses (Cui et al., 2022). Their efficiency decreases when treating 
wastewater containing poorly biodegradable compounds, such as LAS, 
which can compromise effluent quality and microbial stability (Costa 
et al., 2024; Teran et al., 2022). Only 20% of the surfactant is bio­
degraded by anaerobic digestion; the low biodegradation is likely due to 
limited bioavailability resulting from the formation of insoluble chem­
ical species, as well as inhibition of anaerobic biomass activity 
(Terreros-Mecalco et al., 2024).
Granatto et al. (2019) investigated the degradation of LAS from 
domestic sewage in a strictly anaerobic expanded granular sludge bed 
(EGSB) reactor operated at pilot scale. The authors reported an influent 
LAS concentration of 7.4 ± 3.8 mg L−1 associated with an organic 
loading corresponding to 527 ± 233 mg COD L−1 and an HRT of 36 ± 3 
h, resulting in an average LAS removal efficiency of 60 ± 30%. Under 
these operating conditions, the anaerobic process remained microbio­
logically stable, with no significant changes in the microbial community 
structure.
Similarly, Carosia et al. (2014) evaluated LAS biodegradation in an 
anaerobic fluidized-bed (FB) reactor using sand as the support material 
and soap powder as the LAS source. In this study, the influent LAS 
concentration was 14 ± 3 mg L−1, with an associated organic load of 
532 ± 69 mg COD L−1 and an HRT of 15 h, resulting in an average LAS 
removal of 48 ± 10%. However, the higher LAS concentration exerted 
inhibitory effects on different microbial functional groups, as reflected 
in the accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs), suggesting an 
imbalance between acidogenic and methanogenic activities and 
evidencing the sensitivity of anaerobic metabolic pathways to elevated 
surfactant loads.
Given the relevance of LAS and the importance of anaerobic treat­
ment, strategies that enhance its degradation without affecting micro­
bial balance or biogas production are highly valuable. In this context, 
the use of redox mediators has emerged as a promising approach to 
overcome the limitations of biodegradation of structurally complex 
compounds in anaerobic environments (Zhang et al., 2020).
Redox mediators are chemical compounds that enhance extracellular 
electron transfer between anaerobic microorganisms and electron ac­
ceptors or donors, thereby increasing the biodegradation rates of 
recalcitrant pollutants (do Nascimento et al., 2021b). Quinone-based 
mediators 
such 
as 
anthraquinone-2-sulfonate 
(AQS) 
and 
anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate (AQDS) have attracted considerable 
attention due to their reversible redox behavior, low toxicity, and 
chemical stability under anaerobic conditions. These compounds act as 
electron shuttles by accepting reducing equivalents from microbial 
metabolism and subsequently transferring them to target contaminants, 
thereby accelerating reductive transformation pathways already 
demonstrated for dyes, chlorinated compounds, and polycyclic aromatic 
hydrocarbons (He et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018).
In the specific case of linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, AQS may 
interact with distinct structural moieties of the molecule, particularly 
the sulfonate group and the hydrophobic alkyl chain. The reduced form 
of AQS can facilitate electron transfer to the aromatic ring and the sul­
fonate substituent, promoting reductive weakening of the carbon-sulfur 
bond and favoring desulfonation as an initial step in LAS degradation 
(Wu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). In parallel, enhanced electron 
availability may stimulate reductive reactions along the alkyl chain, 
facilitating chain scission and subsequent shortening of the hydrophobic 
moiety, which increases molecular polarity and bioavailability (Palmer 
and Hatley, 2018; Van der Zee and Cervantes, 2009). By mediating these 
key reductive steps, AQS can lower the kinetic and thermodynamic 
barriers to LAS transformation under anaerobic conditions, thereby 
supporting more efficient conversion of LAS into intermediates that are 
more amenable to further anaerobic or syntrophic degradation.
Lu et al. (2021) noticed an increase of 15% of azo dye RR X–3B 
removal when AQS was used during the treatment of synthetic waste­
water in up-flow anaerobic reactors. He et al. (2017) conducted anaer­
obic batch tests with synthetic wastewater containing 10 μg L−1 of the 
antibiotic sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and found that only 10 μM of AQDS 
enhanced contaminant removal by approximately 50%.
LAS aeration biodegradation is energy-intensive due to the high 
oxygen (O2) requirements (Liu et al., 2018), and traditional direct 
aeration can lead to serious foaming problems (Zhang et al., 2023). In 
this regard, introducing low doses of oxygen via microaeration into 
anaerobic systems may be advantageous. Controlled oxygen inputs 
stimulate facultative microbial populations, promote partial oxidation 
of xenobiotics, and facilitate subsequent anaerobic degradation, all 
while maintaining conditions favorable for biogas production (Li et al., 
2024).
Microaeration has shown promising results in removing recalcitrant 
pollutants. Collectively, previous studies have demonstrated that 
introducing low levels of oxygen into anaerobic systems can substan­
tially enhance the removal of a wide range of recalcitrant and micro­
pollutant compounds. Siqueira et al. (2018) observed that, for BTEX 
compounds, microaeration rates of 0.5–2.0 mL air⋅min−1 resulted in 
removal efficiencies above 83%, with benzene removal increasing by 
about 30% compared to strictly anaerobic conditions. Extending this 
concept to pharmaceutical compounds, Buakaew and Ratanatamskul 
(2024) reported that microaeration in an AnBB-MBR treating domestic 
wastewater markedly enhanced antibiotic removal, achieving 78% for 
ciprofloxacin and 88–91% for sulfamethoxazole, substantially out­
performing the non-aerated reactor.
In line with these findings, Carvalho et al. (2020) showed that 
microaeration greatly improved the removal of recalcitrant pollutants in 
anaerobic treatment systems; in a microaerated upflow anaerobic sludge 
blanket (UASB) reactor treating textile wastewater containing the dye 
DB22, complete removal of aromatic amines was achieved, and effluent 
toxicity was reduced 16-fold compared to the strictly anaerobic reactor,

(2021b) reported that, in a UASB reactor treating micropollutants such 
as hormones and pharmaceuticals, an airflow of 4 mL min−1 increased 
removal to 90–94%. In contrast, anaerobic treatment alone achieved less 
than 30%.
To the best of our knowledge, the application of either microaeration 
or AQS in anaerobic systems specifically for LAS removal has not yet 
been explored. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the 
effect of AQS on LAS removal in UASB reactors operated at low HRT, 
typical of full-scale sewage treatment in tropical regions. Operation at 
low HRTs increases volumetric organic and LAS loading rates, imposing 
stronger kinetic and redox constraints on anaerobic biomass. Under 
these conditions, LAS degradation is often limited by inefficient electron 
transfer and the accumulation of partially transformed intermediates, 
leading to low and unstable removal efficiencies. These limitations are 
intensified by the high demand for reducing equivalents associated with 
surfactant biodegradation. Within this framework, AQS and controlled 
microaeration were investigated as complementary strategies to alle­
viate electron transfer bottlenecks and expand the redox flexibility of the 
granular sludge. By facilitating extracellular electron shuttling and 
enabling additional redox pathways, these approaches were hypothe­
sized to enhance LAS transformation and improve reactor stability under 
realistic low-HRT conditions.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental set-up
Two lab-scale UASB reactors (working volume of 3.5 L) (Fig. 1), 
inoculated with anaerobic sludge [Total solids (TS) = 50 ± 3 g L−1, total 
volatile solids (TVS) = 28 ± 1 = g⋅L−1 and total fixed solids (TFS) = 23 
± 1 g L−1], were operated, in parallel, at an HRT of 8 h and room 
temperature of approximately 28 ◦C.
Both reactors operated under the same conditions except for 
microaeration. R1 was a conventional UASB reactor, while R2 included 
microaeration and was called UMSB (Upflow Microaerobic Sludge 
Blanket). The experiment had two 45-day periods, differing only in the 
addition of AQS. In Period I, no AQS was added (R1AQS- and R2AQS-). In 
Period II, both systems (R1AQS+, R2AQS+) were supplemented with 50 
μM AQS (98%, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) to evaluate its impact on system 
performance. This structured approach allowed for a systematic com­
parison of the effects of AQS matter degradation and LAS removal under 
both anaerobic and microaerobic conditions.
Microaeration in R2 was performed with synthetic air (80% N2:20% 
O2, White Martins, Brazil) at its base by means of a mass flow controller 
(GFC17, Cole-Parmer, USA). The microaeration air dose used in R2 was 
approximately 1.0 Lair⋅min−1, corresponding to 0.2 LO2⋅Lfeed
−1 ⋅d−1, which 
was kept constant during the experimental period.
The microaeration rate and the AQS concentration were defined 
based on previous studies conducted by our research group, in which 
these values proved effective in stimulating electron transfer processes 
in aromatic compounds, without causing oxidative stress or toxicity to 
the anaerobic biomass (de Barros et al., 2018; Buarque et al., 2019).
The reactors were fed with synthetic wastewater containing the LAS 
(Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate, 100%, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) (15 mg 
L−1), sucrose (1 gCOD⋅L−1), basal medium (macro and micronutrients) 
prepared according to Firmino et al. (2010), and sodium bicarbonate (1 
g L−1) to maintain the pH close to 7.0. All reagents were used as pur­
chased without further purification. The synthetic influent was kept 
refrigerated at 4 ◦C to prevent natural biodegradation of organic matter.
2.2. Chemical and chromatographic analysis
Chemical oxygen demand (COD), pH, TSS, and TS content were 
determined according to APHA (2012).
The quantification of CH4, CO2, H2, and H2S in the biogas was 
determined by gas chromatography with ionization detection by 
dielectric barrier discharge (GC BID-2010 Plus, Shimadzu Corporation, 
Japan), equipped with a GS-GASPRO column (60 m × 0.32 mm) (Agilent 
Technologies Inc., USA). Helium gas was used as the carrier gas (White 
Martins LTDA, Brazil) at a flow rate of 2 mL min−1, with a run time of 9 
min. Oven, injector, and detector temperatures were 50, 100, and 
250 ◦C, respectively. O2 and N2 were quantified by gas chromatography 
with thermal conductivity detection (GC-TCD) (GC-17A, Shimadzu 
Corporation, Japan). The biogas sample (1.0 mL) was injected in split­
less mode, and chromatographic separation was performed on a Mol 
Sieve 5A PLOT column (30 m, 0.32 mm ID) (Restek Corporation, USA). 
Oven, injector, and detector temperatures were 35, 40, and 230 ◦C, 
respectively. Helium (White Martins, Brazil) was used as the carrier gas 
at a flow rate of 7 mL min−1, and the run time was 5 min.
LAS concentrations were determined by high-performance liquid 
chromatography (HPLC) using a Shimadzu system (CBM-20A, SPD-20A, 
CTO-20A, SIL-20A, and LC-20AT) equipped with a reversed-phase C18 
column from Shimadzu, as described by Silva et al. (2017). The mobile 
phase was water with 5 mmol L−1 ammonium acetate (solvent A) and 
acetonitrile (solvent B); the mobile phase flow rate was 1 mL min−1, the 
sample volume was 50 μL, the temperature of the thermostated 
compartment of the column was 40 ◦C, and UV-Vis detection at 230 nm. 
A gradient was applied to the mobile phase to separate the LAS con­
stituents; it started at 45% solvent B, which began to rise after 5 min and 
reached 60% in 20 min, then returned to 45% after 1 min and remained 
at 45% for 6 min.
Biomass samples from the inoculum and the four reactors were sent 
to identify microbial communities and underwent extraction, 
sequencing, and analysis of absolute abundances. DNA collection, 
extraction, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and data processing 
were performed following the methodology described by Silva et al. 
(2023). The sequencing data generated in this study have been sub­
mitted to the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) 
BioProject repository under the ID PRJNA836880.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the UASB reactors
3.1.1. Operational parameters and volumetric biogas production
The evaluation of operational pH and acidity parameters in the UASB 
reactors, both with and without microaeration, revealed very similar 
values, regardless of AQS use (Fig. 2). The average pH remained be­
tween 7.4 and 7.6 throughout the experimental period, with no signif­
icant differences between reactors. Acidity/TA ratios ranged from 0.54 
± 0.09 to 0.82 ± 1.06, and during the stabilization phase, they were 
further stabilized, with all values falling below the threshold of 0.8 
typically associated with process imbalance.
Therefore, the application of AQS and controlled microaeration did 
not cause acid-base disturbances or instability in either pH or Acidity/ 
TA. This suggests that these strategies are compatible with the physi­
cochemical equilibrium required for anaerobic treatment systems and 
do not compromise reactor stability when applied at moderate doses. In 
the study by do Nascimento et al. (2021b), microaeration (1 mL air­
⋅min−1) combined with the redox mediator AQDS (50–100 μM) also 
maintained system stability, with the oxidation-reduction potential 
(ORP) remaining below −200 mV, ensuring conditions suitable for 
reductive biotransformation.
Fig. 3 presents the volumetric production of biogas and methane for 
each UASB reactor over the experimental period. Reactors R1AQS- and 
R1AQS+ (anaerobic conditions, without and with AQS) showed similar 
patterns (p = 0.064), with average methane yields of 2.0 ± 0.2 L/day 
and 1.9 ± 0.3 L/day, respectively. The methane fraction in the biogas 
from these reactors was stable and consistent with expected values for 
anaerobic digestion of readily biodegradable substrates, averaging 67.2 
± 2.7% (R1AQS-) and 67.6 ± 2.7% (R1AQS+) (p = 0.026). These results 
indicate a predominance of methanogenic activity and suggest that 
adding AQS under strictly anaerobic conditions did not adversely affect 
methane production.
In contrast, reactors R2AQS- and R2AQS+, which received microaera­
tion (without and with AQS), produced significantly higher volumes of 
biogas and methane (p < 0.05). The total volumetric methane produc­
tion reached 4.9 ± 0.6 L/day in R2 and 5.6 ± 0.7 L/day in R2AQS+, 
indicating a substantial increase in overall gas production compared to 
anaerobic treatments. However, these increases were accompanied by a 
marked reduction in the methane content of the biogas, which averaged 
only 31.9 ± 4.3% (R2AQS-) and 33.5 ± 4.3% (R2AQS+). These values are 
less than half of those observed in the strictly anaerobic reactors.
This inverse relationship between total biogas production and 
methane concentration is more consistently explained by the presence of 
oxygen in the microaerated reactors, which altered gas composition 
through multiple coupled mechanisms rather than solely by nitrogen 
dilution. The supplied oxygen was likely consumed by facultative and 
aerobic microorganisms, promoting partial oxidation of reduced com­
pounds and increasing CO2 formation, thereby reducing the volumetric 
fraction of methane in the biogas. In addition, oxygen availability may 
have redirected part of the electron flow away from strict methano­
genesis toward alternative respiratory pathways, thereby affecting 
methane yield without necessarily reducing overall biogas generation.
In this context, Buarque et al. (2019) highlighted that low oxygen 
concentrations in anaerobic systems promote partial oxidation of sub­
strates, favoring biomass growth and alternative metabolic pathways 
while decreasing methane production efficiency. Consistent with this 
trade-off between pollutant removal and energy recovery, several 
studies have reported that microaeration can enhance contaminant 
degradation at the expense of methane yield. For example, Guimar˜aes de 
Oliveira et al. (2021), evaluating the effect of microaeration in a UASB 
reactor treating swine wastewater (2.0 mL air⋅L feed−1), observed that 
no methane was detected in the biogas from the UMSB reactor, a result 
attributed to methane dilution by other gases due to the continuous 
injection of atmospheric air. Despite the reduction in methane content, 
the increase in absolute methane volume in R2AQS- and R2AQS + suggests 
that methanogenesis was not suppressed. Instead, a portion of the 
organic load was likely directed to oxidative metabolism or assimilated 
into new biomass, while the remainder continued to be converted into 
methane.
The application of AQS in R2AQS+, when combined with microaer­
ation, resulted in similar methane yields across all treatments (p > 0.05). 
This behavior is consistent with previous findings by do Nascimento 
et al. (2021b), who demonstrated that the introduction of microaeration 
in UASB reactors increases total biogas production while reducing the 
methane volumetric fraction due to gas dilution, without compromising 
the biogas energetic quality. Their results support the interpretation that 
microaeration modifies biogas composition primarily through changes 
in gas balance rather than through inhibition of methanogenic activity, 
consistent with the trends observed in the present study.
Moreover, the decrease in methane concentration does not neces­
sarily indicate process instability or inhibition of anaerobic metabolism. 
The observed shift in biogas composition is better interpreted as a 
combined effect of methane dilution by increased CO2 production and 
the potential for biological methane oxidation in microaerobic niches 
within the reactor. These processes are consistent with the gas compo­
sition data and suggest that microaeration primarily modified carbon 
flow and redox balance rather than compromising the stability of the 
anaerobic treatment process.

At the same time, the presence of a redox mediator does not affect the 
production and/or composition of biogas. In this context, while volu­
metric methane production can be maintained or even increased, the 
biogas quality, in terms of methane concentration, may be compro­
mised. Further research into optimizing oxygen dosing and mediator 
concentration could help balance these outcomes, aiming for enhanced 
pollutant removal without significant loss in methane purity.
3.1.2. Efficiency parameters
The COD removal efficiency and the specific methane yield per unit 
of applied organic load are presented in Fig. 4. All reactors achieved 
high COD removal efficiencies, exceeding 80%, indicating effective 
conversion of organic matter under all operational conditions. In re­
actors R1AQS- and R1AQS+ (anaerobic, with and without AQS), average 
COD removals were 82.3 ± 8.0% and 84.9 ± 7.3%, respectively, 
showing that the addition of AQS alone did not significantly impact the 
degradation of bulk organic matter (p > 0.05).
Reactors R2AQS- and R2AQS+, which received microaeration, pre­
sented higher COD removal efficiencies (p < 0.05) of 86.5 ± 4.3% and

particularly when combined with AQS in R2AQS+. The elevated perfor­
mance in R2AQS + may result from synergistic effects between oxygen

aerobic and anaerobic metabolic routes, favoring the degradation of 
more complex or partially oxidized intermediates (Buakaew and Rata­

However, when COD removal is analyzed alongside methane pro­
duction, a distinct trend emerges. The specific methane production 
(LCH4/gCODapp) was significantly lower (p < 0.05) in anaerobic reactors 
(0.19 ± 0.05 in R1AQS- and 0.17 ± 0.04 in R1AQS+) compared to the 
microaerated systems (0.46 ± 0.08 in R2AQS- and 0.50 ± 0.11 in 
R2AQS+).
This apparent contradiction can be explained by the fact that while 
oxygen presence reduced the methane percentage in the biogas, it did 
not reduce total methane generation relative to organic load. On the 
contrary, microaeration likely stimulated faster and more complete 
substrate degradation, leading to greater methane volumes per gram of 
COD applied, especially in R2AQS+, where the AQS may have facilitated 
redox reactions essential for the breakdown of intermediate products. 
Similar effects have been reported in anaerobic reactors treating anti­
biotics and aromatic compounds using AQS and AQDS, where the redox 
mediator enhanced electron transfer and accelerated rate-limiting steps 
(Buakaew and Ratanatamskul, 2024; dos Santos et al., 2007).
Furthermore, these results suggest that although a portion of the 
COD may have been consumed via oxidative pathways or biomass 
synthesis under microaerobic conditions, a substantial fraction still 
followed the methanogenic route, particularly in the presence of AQS. 
The performance of R2AQS + thus highlights the potential of combining 
microaeration and redox mediation to achieve both high removal effi­
ciency and energy recovery in UASB systems.
Finally, the greater consistency observed in the boxplots for both 
COD removal and methane yield in R2AQS + supports the reproducibility 
of this combined strategy. Compared to R1AQS- and R1AQS+, the lower 
variability in R2AQS + may indicate a more stable and resilient microbial 
community, better adapted to simultaneous oxygen exposure and redox 
cycling – an aspect further explored in Section 3.3.
3.2. Removal of linear alkylbenzene sulfonate
3.2.1. Effect of microaeration
In the first days of operation, the four reactors showed average LAS 
removal efficiencies of around 79 ± 1%, with no statistically significant 
differences between the systems (p > 0.05) (Fig. 5). This initial behavior 
can be attributed to the greater functional diversity of the newly 
established anaerobic microbiota, as populations are not yet under the 
selective pressure of sulfonated compounds. At this stage, the lower 
accumulation of toxic intermediates and the absence of prolonged stress 
are likely to favor greater activity of consortia capable of degrading 
xenobiotic compounds such as LAS, even if only partially.
In addition, LAS concentrations had not yet reached critical inhibi­
tion levels, which may have allowed secondary or nonspecific metabolic 
pathways to act in its initial transformation. Among these mechanisms, 
the action of nonspecific oxidoreductases stands out, which, according 
to Zhou et al. (2022) and Costa et al. (2024), can actively participate in 
the biodegradation of surfactants such as LAS by promoting oxidation 
and reduction reactions that are not very selective but effective in 
initially breaking the aromatic structure and aliphatic chain of these 
compounds. Similarly, Li et al. (2024) observed that UASB reactors 
showed high efficiency in removing sodium dodecylbenzene sulfonate (a 
type of LAS) during the first days of operation, with initial values around 
80%, which decreased to less than 20% after 120 days.
Throughout the operation, reactors not subjected to microaeration 
(R1AQS- and R1AQS+) exhibited greater operational instability in LAS 
removal, with more pronounced fluctuations in degradation efficiency 
and a progressive downward trend, especially in the system without 
AQS (R1AQS-). R1AQS- showed the worst performance in LAS removal, 
with a continuous downward trend until reaching final valuesclose to 
11%. This instability may be related to the metabolic limitation imposed 
by a strictly anaerobic environment in the face of highly recalcitrant 
compounds, such as LAS. In the absence of oxygen, LAS degradation 
depends exclusively on less efficient anaerobic pathways, which are 
often incapable of breaking the sulfonated aromatic ring, leading to the 
accumulation of toxic intermediates or the interruption of metabolic 
pathways (Corada-Fern´andez et al., 2018). The lack of microaeration 
also compromises the development of niches for facultative or micro­
aerophilic microorganisms (Castro et al., 2023; do Nascimento et al., 
2021a), which could complement surfactant degradation through par­
tial oxidative processes, thereby contributing to greater system stability.
The systems subjected to microaeration showed significantly higher 
and more stable LAS removals over time than reactors operated under 
strictly anaerobic conditions (p < 0.001). In particular, the R2AQS- 
reactor, microaerated and without a redox mediator, achieved an 
average removal of 70 ± 3%, while the R1AQS- reactor, operated without 
microaeration and without AQS, showed lower removal, with an

even at very low concentrations, is decisive for the degradation of sur­

aerobic pathway as the main transformation route of this compound

The introduction of microaeration into anaerobic systems has been 
reported to enhance the biodegradation of surfactants and other 
difficult-to-biodegrade compounds. Cheng et al. (2018) reduced the 
surfactant concentration from 9000 mg/L to 2000 mg/L without foam 
formation or significant VFAs mineralization. Carvalho et al. (2020)
achieved complete removal of the azo dye Direct Black 22 with 
microaeration in the UASB reactor.
The action of microaerobic pathways also contributes to maintaining 
a more dynamic redox environment, in which fermentative, reducing, 
and oxidative processes coexist, increasing metabolic diversity and, 
consequently, the system's resilience in the presence of recalcitrant 
compounds (do Nascimento et al., 2021b; Fu et al., 2023). Therefore, 
microaeration promotes not only greater efficiency but also greater 
stability in LAS removal, as evidenced by the low variability in results 
obtained in R2AQS-.
3.2.2. Impact of anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) supplementation
The addition of the redox mediator anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) 
resulted in significant increases in LAS removal in both systems, 
demonstrating the fundamental role of this compound in enhancing 
electron transfer and overcoming limiting steps in LAS biodegradation. 
Despite this, the microaerated reactor with AQS (R2AQS+) showed the 
best overall performance, with an average removal of 77 ± 1%, signif­
icantly higher than that observed in the reactor also doped with AQS, 
but operated without microaeration (R1AQS+), which obtained 65 ± 4% 
(p < 0.001).
AQS functions as an extracellular redox mediator, promoting elec­
tron transfer between microorganisms and substrates and yielding very 
satisfactory results in systems treating highly recalcitrant compounds, 
such as LAS (Ren et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020). The beneficial effect of 
quinone-based redox mediators is not restricted to inorganic or surfac­
tant pollutants. For instance, do Nascimento et al. (2021b) observed an 
increase in antibiotic removal from 6% to 75% upon the addition of such 
mediators. In line with these findings, Tang et al. (2024) also reported an 
improvement in the denitrification rate in the presence of quinone-type 
redox mediators.
In this context, AQS is highly stable and can alternate between its 
oxidized (quinone) and reduced (hydroquinone) forms, facilitating 
redox reactions in conditions where microorganisms have limited direct 
electron transfer (Ren et al., 2022). Therefore, during LAS degradation, 
the presence of AQS can facilitate desulfonation and promote aromatic 
ring breakdown, favoring the formation of metabolites more accessible 
to anaerobic and facultative aerobic pathways.
This behavior becomes evident when the operational performance of 
the different reactors is examined comparatively. Under strictly anaer­
obic conditions, AQS addition increased LAS removal without substan­
tially affecting methane production, indicating that the redox mediator 
primarily facilitated contaminant transformation rather than altering 
the overall digestion pathway. Conversely, microaeration alone 
improved reactor stability and organic matter removal but led to fluc­
tuating LAS removal at lower levels. When both strategies were applied 
simultaneously in reactor R2AQS+, higher LAS removal was achieved, 
along with increased methane production and improved COD removal. 
This concurrent improvement in multiple performance indicators sug­
gests that microaeration and AQS influenced complementary stages of 
the LAS degradation process.
Low oxygen availability likely promoted initial activation or condi­
tioning of the surfactant structure, while AQS enhanced subsequent 
reductive steps by facilitating electron transfer, thereby preventing the 
accumulation of inhibitory intermediates. As a result, the combined 
operation led to a process response that exceeds what would be expected 
from the individual effects of microaeration or AQS alone, supporting 
the interpretation of a synergistic interaction at the process level.
Although AQS promoted significant gains in LAS removal in both 
systems, its effect was more pronounced in the conventional UASB 
reactor operated without microaeration. In R1AQS+, the presence of the 
mediator resulted in a removal efficiency about twice that of the control 
reactor without AQS (R1AQS-), increasing the average from 32 ± 16% to 
65 ± 4%. On the other hand, in the system with microaeration (R2AQS+), 
the increase provided by the AQS was proportionally smaller, reaching 
only about 10% compared to the microaerated reactor without mediator 
(R2AQS-), which achieved 70 ± 3%. These results indicate that although 
the AQS significantly intensified LAS biodegradation, especially under 
strictly anaerobic conditions, it was not sufficient to match the removal 
levels achieved by systems with oxygen supply (p = 0.017).
The difference observed between the systems reinforces the limita­
tion imposed by the absence of oxygen in strictly anaerobic environ­
ments, which restricts the action of oxidative pathways essential for LAS 
degradation. Although the AQS increased electron transfer and pro­
moted partial transformation of the molecule, the opening of the aro­
matic ring and desulfonation, which are key steps in its mineralization, 
remain strongly dependent on reactions that require molecular oxygen. 
Thus, even with the addition of the mediator, the performance of the 
R1AQS + reactor did not match that of the microaerated system without 
AQS (R2AQS-), whose greater LAS removal highlights the central role of 
microaeration in enabling more effective biochemical pathways for 
recalcitrant compounds such as sulfonated surfactants.
do Nascimento et al. (2021b) also observed significant gains in 
antibiotic removal when combining AQS with microaeration in UASB 
reactors. However, the authors point out that, from a technical stand­
point, diluting biogas and the associated costs may not justify its use.
In summary, the absence of microaeration prevented the formation 
of intermediate redox zones, thereby hindering the partial oxidation or 
desulfonation of LAS. Even with the presence of AQS, which favored 
mediated electron-transfer pathways and were essential for accelerating 
the rate-limiting steps of biodegradation, the absence of microaeration 
prevented the formation of intermediate redox zones. Therefore, 
although AQS represents an important technological resource for 
increasing the efficiency of anaerobic reactors, its effect is limited when 
isolated from a more favorable redox environment. The persistence of 
LAS in anaerobic systems, even in the presence of redox mediators, 
underscores the need for integrated strategies, such as combining 
microaeration with AQS addition, to efficiently treat recalcitrant anionic 
surfactants in UASB reactors.
3.3. Microbial community composition
3.3.1. Microbial community richness and diversity
Microbial richness and diversity were evaluated using Chao1 and 
ACE as estimators of species richness and Shannon and inverse Simpson 
indices as complementary measures of diversity, integrating richness 
and evenness. As shown in Fig. 6, the observed patterns indicate that 
microaeration and AQS affected microbial communities differently, 
helping explain the contrasting behaviors observed in LAS removal.
The markedly higher Chao1 and ACE values in R2AQS- and R2AQS +
compared to the strictly anaerobic reactors indicate that microaeration 
was the dominant driver of species recruitment. The introduction of 
oxygen, even at low levels, likely promoted niche diversification by 
allowing the coexistence of strict anaerobes, facultative, and micro­
aerophilic populations (Buarque et al., 2019; do Nascimento et al., 
2021b). This expansion of ecological niches increases the probability of 
functional redundancy and metabolic complementarity, particularly

The consistently lower richness observed in R2AQS + relative to

Although Shannon indices were similar between R2AQS- and R2AQS+, 
the inverse Simpson index clearly differentiated these reactors, indi­
cating distinct community organization patterns. The similarity in 
Shannon values suggests that overall diversity, when weighted toward 
rare taxa, remained comparable. In contrast, the lower inverse Simpson 
value in R2AQS + indicates reduced evenness and increased dominance of 
specific populations. This pattern is consistent with the enrichment of 
functionally specialized groups, likely including methanogenic archaea 
and bacteria involved in redox-active metabolisms, which become 
competitively favored in the presence of an efficient electron shuttle 
such as AQS. Therefore, while richness was preserved, community 
structure shifted toward dominance by taxa with higher energetic effi­

Under strictly anaerobic conditions, both Shannon and inverse 
Simpson indices were lower and largely unaffected by AQS addition, 
reinforcing that, in the absence of microaeration, AQS primarily acted at 
the metabolic level rather than reshaping community diversity. In these 
reactors, LAS degradation was likely constrained by kinetic and ther­
modynamic limitations, and the redox mediator alone was insufficient to 
trigger broad ecological restructuring.
The combined analysis of diversity indices suggests that enhanced 
LAS removal in R2AQS + cannot be attributed solely to increased richness 
or generalized microbial adaptation. Instead, the data support a scenario 
in which AQS selectively amplified the activity and relative abundance 
of key functional groups that enable coupling of LAS transformation to 
efficient electron transfer pathways. By facilitating electron flow from 
LAS-derived intermediates toward terminal electron acceptors, AQS 
likely reduced energetic bottlenecks associated with sulfonate reduction 
and alkyl chain transformation, conferring a competitive advantage to 
specialized degraders. Consequently, LAS removal was improved 
through a synergy between microaeration-driven niche expansion and 
AQS-mediated functional selection, rather than through a simple in­
crease in overall microbial diversity, as observed in other studies (do 
Nascimento et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022).
3.3.2. Microbial community structure
The microbial community structure exhibited consistent, process- 
relevant shifts across the reactors, closely mirroring the observed dif­
ferences in LAS removal, methane production, and overall process sta­
bility (Fig. 7 and 8). At the domain level, Bacteria predominated in all 
systems, reflecting their central role in hydrolysis, fermentation, and the 
initial transformation of complex substrates such as LAS. However, 
pronounced variations in the relative abundance of Archaea highlight 
that AQS addition and microaeration exerted strong selective pressures 
on electron flow and syntrophic organization, rather than merely 
increasing microbial diversity.
In the strictly anaerobic reactor without AQS (R1AQS-), Bacteria 
accounted for 72.0% of the community. Despite presenting the highest 
methane fraction in the biogas, this reactor showed the poorest and most 
unstable LAS removal. At the phylum level, Firmicutes and Actino­
bacteriota dominated, while at the family and genus levels, Bogoriellaceae 
and Georgenia were prominent. These taxa are typically associated with 
hydrolytic and fermentative metabolism and, in some cases, facultative 
behavior. Their dominance suggests a community well adapted to con­
ventional anaerobic digestion but poorly structured to sustain reductive

flux (do Nascimento et al., 2021b; Van der Zee and Cervantes, 2009).
Microaeration alone (R2AQS-) increased richness and promoted the 
coexistence of strict anaerobes and facultative microorganisms, consis­
tent with previous reports (Buarque et al., 2019; do Nascimento et al., 
2021b). At the phylum level, Euryarchaeota became more prominent, 
while at the family level, Anaerolineaceae and Eubacteriaceae increased 
in relative abundance, reflecting reinforcement of syntrophic and 
fermentative networks. However, despite improved COD removal and 
increased total biogas production, LAS removal remained unstable. This 
indicates that microaeration enhanced metabolic flexibility and resil­

electron flow toward LAS-specific reductive pathways.
The synergistic effect of AQS and microaeration was most evident in 
R2AQS+, which exhibited the highest archaeal abundance (43.9%) and 
the best overall process performance. At the phylum and class levels, 
Euryarchaeota and Methanobacteria dominated, with Methanobacteria 
reaching approximately 40.0%. At the family and genus levels, Meth­
anobacteriaceae and Methanobacterium were strongly enriched, high­
lighting the central role of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. The rapid 
consumption of hydrogen by these archaea is critical for maintaining 
low redox potential and preventing feedback inhibition of fermentative 
and syntrophic bacteria, thereby sustaining continuous LAS trans­
formation (Li et al., 2022).
In parallel, the enrichment of syntrophic bacterial families such as 
Anaerolineaceae and Eubacteriaceae, along with the dominance of the 
unclassified genus midas g_2229 in R1AQS+ and R2AQS+, indicates the 
establishment of a highly integrated syntrophic network. These taxa are 
frequently associated with the anaerobic degradation of long-chain 
hydrocarbons and surfactants and rely on close metabolic coupling with 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens (do Nascimento et al., 2021b; Van der 
Zee and Cervantes, 2009; Motteran et al., 2022). In contrast, the 
exclusive dominance of Georgenia in R1AQS- reflects a population less 
competitive under conditions favoring mediated electron transfer and 
syntrophic specialization.
Overall, the taxonomic and functional patterns demonstrate that 
efficient and stable LAS removal was governed by synergistic in­
teractions between microaeration and AQS rather than by microbial 
diversity or methane content alone. Microaeration expanded ecological 
niches and enhanced metabolic robustness, while AQS selectively 
facilitated electron exchange between LAS-degrading bacteria and 
methanogenic archaea. The convergence of these effects in R2AQS +
promoted a microbial community highly specialized for coordinated 
electron flow, explaining the superior LAS removal, enhanced COD 
degradation, and increased methane production observed under this 
condition.
3.4. Impact of anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) supplementation and 
microaeration
The improved LAS removal observed in the AQS-amended reactors 
corroborates the role of quinone-based redox mediators in facilitating 
the transformation of recalcitrant sulfonated compounds through 
enhanced extracellular electron transfer. Nevertheless, the performance 
of R2AQS + indicates that reactor redox conditions modulated the effect 
of AQS. While AQS addition alone (R1AQS+) increased LAS removal 
without major shifts in microbial diversity, its combination with 
microaeration led to a microbial community characterized by higher 
richness, altered evenness patterns, and the enrichment of taxa capable 
of functioning under low-oxygen conditions. This configuration supports 
a degradation scheme in which microaeration expands metabolic func­
tionality and ecological niches, whereas AQS improves electron transfer 
efficiency within this diversified community. Importantly, the absence 
of process instability or inhibition suggests that oxygen was rapidly 
consumed in non-methanogenic pathways, preserving anaerobic 
functionality.
Although direct identification of LAS intermediates was beyond the 
scope of this study, the consistent association between enhanced LAS 
removal, distinct microbial structuring, and combined redox manipu­
lation provides process-level evidence that microaeration and AQS 
interacted synergistically to improve LAS degradation.
From an operational perspective, however, microaeration demands 
strict control. Oxygen must be dosed at levels sufficient for enzyme-level 
activation but low enough to avoid its escape to the headspace, where it 
would compromise biogas combustion safety by altering the flamma­
bility range. Maintaining this balance is challenging because real-time 
dissolved oxygen monitoring in anaerobic systems remains unreliable, 
and commercial DO sensors often exhibit poor sensitivity at the micro­
aerobic range required for mediators and surfactant transformation. 
Thus, control strategies based on the system's redox potential become 
particularly attractive. Because AQS actively participates in redox 
cycling, monitoring the reactor's redox potential provides a more 
mechanistic and responsive basis for adjusting aeration, avoiding oxy­
gen accumulation, and optimizing mediator performance.
Despite these advantages, the continuous addition of soluble AQS 
increases operational costs and generates concerns for downstream 
treatment, especially if residual mediator exits with the effluent. For full- 
scale applications, this limitation has driven interest in immobilized 
mediator systems. Activated carbon, biochar, and engineered nano­
materials containing quinone-rich functional groups can retain the 
mediator within the reactor, provide long-term electron-shuttling ca­
pacity, and substantially reduce the demand for repeated dosing (Zhang 
et al., 2020). Such materials also align with practical anaerobic treat­
ment constraints by simplifying operation and lowering chemical con­
sumption while preserving the enhanced LAS degradation observed in

4. Conclusions
This study demonstrated that the use of anthraquinone-2-sulfonate 
(AQS) as a redox mediator, both alone and in combination with 
microaeration, can enhance the performance of UASB reactors treating 
LAS-containing wastewater and treated at low HRTs. While the appli­
cation of AQS under strictly anaerobic conditions did not significantly 
alter reactor stability or organic matter removal, it promoted the 
enrichment of methanogenic Archaea and selected syntrophic bacterial 
groups, suggesting the development of improved redox-driven biodeg­
radation pathways.
The combination of AQS and microaeration (R2AQS+) yielded the 
highest LAS removal, COD degradation, and methane production per 
unit of applied organic load, indicating a synergistic effect between 
redox mediation and controlled oxygenation. This condition also pro­
moted a more diverse and archaeal-enriched microbial community, 
characterized by the dominance of Methanobacterium and midas_g_2229, 
potentially associated with enhanced LAS degradation under syntrophic 
conditions.
These findings highlight the potential of integrating redox-active 
compounds and low-intensity aeration as a viable strategy to improve 
anaerobic treatment of surfactant-rich wastewaters. Future studies 
should investigate the long-term stability of such systems, assess the fate 
of intermediate metabolites, and explore the functional roles of key 
microbial taxa identified, particularly through metagenomic or tran­
scriptomic approaches.
